title: Caffeine is a pesticide: plants make it to paralyse and kill insects
body: The world’s most widely consumed psychoactive drug wasn’t made for us. Coffee, tea and cacao plants produce caffeine in their seeds, fruits and leaves as a **natural pesticide** that can paralyse and kill insects feeding on them, and coffee seedlings carry high levels while their young leaves have no other protection. Caffeine leaching into the soil also stops rival coffee seedlings from germinating nearby. Plants even put a little in their nectar, where it seems to improve honeybees’ memory of the flower, bringing them back. In us, it works by blocking adenosine, a molecule that tells the brain to slow down.

slides.heading: What caffeine does for the plant
items: Paralyses and kills insects that chew on it
In nectar, boosts pollinators’ memory of the flower
Guards seedlings before they grow tough leaves

slides.label: typical caffeine content of a coffee bean, by weight
slides.text: A 120 ml cup of drip coffee carries roughly 100–125 mg; a cup of tea steeped for three minutes about 22–74 mg.

slides.heading: Why it wakes you up
slides.text: Adenosine is a molecule that signals the brain to slow down and feel sleepy. Caffeine blocks the receptors adenosine binds to, so the signal doesn’t get through. Almost 10 million tonnes of coffee beans were consumed worldwide in 2020.

steps.label: Adenosine builds up during the day
It binds to receptors that say: slow down
The slow-down signal never gets through

slides.question: Why do plants put caffeine in their nectar?
options: To help bees remember the flower
slides.explanation: Caffeine in nectar appears to enhance pollinators’ reward memory, so honeybees are more likely to return to that plant.

slides.clue: The molecule that tells your brain to slow down; caffeine blocks its receptors
slides.detail: Caffeine fits the receptors adenosine would bind to, so the sleepy signal never gets through.
